Sorry, she did. Her key point was that precedents should guide judges, not control them.
Okay, and how did she back that up? She always asks for evidence.
She used two old cases. She pointed out that the court had changed its mind twice in ten years, and she argued that nobody had noticed.
Did anyone disagree? That sounds like the kind of thing Marcus would fight about.
He did. He claimed that a court without fixed rules was dangerous. It was a good counterargument, and she acknowledged that he had a point.

I started well, but I stumbled over the word jurisprudence and trailed off. So I stopped, rephrased it, and I think I finally got my point across.

Her key point was that precedents should guide judges, not control them.
She backed it up with two cases from the last ten years.
Marcus claimed that the court was dangerous, and she acknowledged that he had a point.
Let me rephrase that, because it came out wrong.

When students tell me they stumble over their words, I ask them to summarize something out loud, and almost every time the problem is not vocabulary. The problem is that they try to say everything in one long sentence, so they run out of breath and trail off. A spoken summary needs blocks, not sentences. Block one: who said it, and the main point. Block two: one piece of evidence, only one. Block three: your reaction. Between the blocks, you breathe. And if a word does not come, you do not wait for it. You rephrase and keep going, because the listener cannot see the word you are looking for. They only hear the silence. Try it tonight with anything, a class, a video, a conversation. Thirty seconds, three blocks, and no word is allowed to stop you.

Let us start with a simple question that has divided lawyers for centuries. When a court has already decided a case, should the next court be forced to decide the same way? In the common law tradition, the answer is mostly yes. Earlier decisions, called precedents, give the system something it badly needs: predictability. A company that signs a contract today wants to know how a judge will read it in five years. But precedent has a cost. Societies change faster than courts, and a rule that made sense fifty years ago can produce an unfair result today. That is why higher courts sometimes overrule their own decisions. The real debate, then, is not whether the past should matter. It is how much weight it should carry, and who gets to decide when it is time to let it go.
